catalog_entry.label: MLB season feats (no-hitter, perfect game, 20-win season, 20-K game, 500-ft HR, 4-HR game, grand-slam game, 50/50)
contract_types: Pitcher no-hitter (individual or combined reading unresolved)
catalog_entry.target: Whether any player or pitcher achieves a rare league-wide season feat (a no-hitter, read as individual or combined because the rule says 'any pitcher' while the title says individual; a perfect game, 20 wins, 20 strikeouts in a game, a 500-foot home run, a 4-home-run game, 2 grand slams in a game, or 50 home runs and 50 steals) by season end.
catalog_entry.mechanism: Eight unrelated rare-feat events share one series. Six single-game feats (a no-hitter, whose individual versus combined reading is unresolved so both are carried; a perfect game; a 20-strikeout game; a 4-home-run game; a 2-grand-slam game; a 500-foot home run) are unions over the roughly 4,860 team-games of the regular season plus playoff games, each with a tiny per-game rate set by the league strikeout and power environment, starter length and (for no-hitters and perfect games) defence and official scoring. Two are season-accumulation races among the few individuals on pace: 20 regular-season wins (remaining starts times per-start win credit) and 50 home runs with 50 steals (remaining plate appearances, power, speed and health), each a union over the candidates still alive. A feat that has already happened settles Yes and the markets close on occurrence.

inputs.why: Team-game hazard of each single-game feat (no-hitter, perfect game, 20-K game, 4-HR game, 2-grand-slam game, 500-ft drive), the headline engine for six of the eight events.
Race-state engine for KXMLBSTAT-26W20: probability that any pitcher reaches 20 regular-season wins from wins to date and remaining starts.
Joint power-speed season distribution for the 50 home run / 50 steal event across every hitter on pace.
Physical tail of measured home-run distance behind the 500-foot Statcast event.
Opportunity term for the two-grand-slam game: bases-loaded plate appearances times conversion.
Starter exit hazard sets how many outs one pitcher gets, which gates no-hitter, perfect-game and 20-strikeout chances and win credit.
Strikeout rate of the pitcher and opposing lineup drives the 20-strikeout game tail.
Contact allowed and defence behind the pitcher decide whether a no-hit or perfect game survives balls in play.
Borderline hit-versus-error rulings decide whether a no-hit bid is intact; the scorer is the settlement authority for no-hitters.
Per-PA home-run propensity of power hitters feeds four-home-run games, grand slams and the 50-home-run half of 50/50.
Park, wind, temperature and ball carry scale per-PA home-run rates in the multi-homer and long-distance events.
Rate x PA x games projection supplies each candidate's remaining home runs and steals.
Sprint speed and attempt propensity bound the stolen-base half of 50/50.
Steal-attempt hazard per opportunity converts speed into stolen bases for 50/50 candidates.
Season state (wins and losses to date, games remaining) frames every season-threshold race and the expected remaining team-games.
Remaining starts for each win-race candidate follow from rotation slot, rest and off-day skipping.
Point-in-time IL status removes injured candidates from the 20-win and 50/50 races and from single-game exposure.
Expected playoff team-games add exposure to the six events that count the postseason.
The exact event wording (any pitcher versus any hitter, regular season versus playoffs, no-hitter definition) differs by event and decides what counts.
Feats-to-date ledger: which of the eight events have already occurred in 2026, with candidate counts for the wins and 50/50 races and team games remaining, as of the market timestamp.
Ball, pitch clock and rule regime shift strikeout, home-run and starter-length rates between seasons, and so every per-game feat rate.

interactions.hypothesis: Twenty strikeouts need both a very high strikeout rate per batter and enough batters faced, so the pitcher-level probability is the product of rate and depth; a pitcher with a high strikeout rate who is pulled early, or a deep pitcher with an ordinary rate, contributes little, and the two factors are estimated from different data.
interactions.how_to_test: Across starts since 1990, compare the observed frequency of 15+ strikeout games by cells of pitcher K% and batters faced against the product of the two marginal rates.

interactions.hypothesis: Two grand slams in one game require two bases-loaded plate appearances and two home runs, so the probability is roughly the product of opportunity and conversion squared; a high-power hitter batting behind weak on-base hitters has little opportunity and a mid-power cleanup hitter in a high-scoring game has more.
interactions.how_to_test: Bucket historical hitter-games by number of bases-loaded plate appearances (0, 1, 2+) and compare the observed count of 2+ GS games with the product of opportunity and per-hitter conversion.

interactions.hypothesis: The distance input carries altitude and temperature but not the wind component; a wind blowing out adds distance on top of altitude and exit velocity, and the tail beyond 500 feet is convex in the total shift, so a tailwind at a high-altitude park for a hitter with an extreme exit-velocity ceiling multiplies the chance more than the sum of the separate effects.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare the share of home runs beyond 450 feet by wind-out component within park-altitude and exit-velocity-tier cells, and test whether the odds ratio of the wind term grows with altitude.

interactions.hypothesis: A candidate with W0 wins and n starts left can only reach 20 if W0 + n >= 20, and realistically if the needed win rate is attainable; late in the season the probability drops to zero in steps as candidates are eliminated, and an injury or skipped start removes starts in one jump.
interactions.how_to_test: Replay 2015-2025 seasons date by date and check that the model's P(any >= 20) is zero for dates when no candidate satisfies W0 + remaining starts >= 20.

contract.settlement_definition: KXMLBSTAT lists eight non-velocity events (Kalshi events API, retrieved 2026-11-09, saved in evidence_zblk/MLB_kxmlbstat_events.json; this wording was NOT part of the sampled rules file). Single-game feats settle YES if any pitcher records a perfect game or a no hitter, any pitcher records 20+ strikeouts in a game, any hitter records 4+ home runs in a game, 2+ grand slams in a game, or a 500+ foot home run '(per Statcast measurement)', in any game during the 2026 season (regular season and playoffs). Season thresholds settle YES if any pitcher records 20+ wins, or any hitter records 50+ home runs and 50+ steals, across all games of the 2026 regular season only. The only rules text sampled for KXMLBSTAT is the velocity event 'If any pitcher records a 107+ MPH Pitch in any game during the 2026 Pro Baseball season (regular season and playoffs)', which uses the same any-player union and season-plus-playoffs window as the single-game feats; for the other events the one-sentence wording above is all that was retrieved, and rules_secondary is only the generic disclaimer. Not defined anywhere: what counts as a no-hitter (combined, nine innings, shortened games), rounding of the Statcast distance, treatment of suspended games and the scoring authority. The event title says 'Individual Pitcher No Hitter' while the rule says 'any pitcher records a no hitter'; the two disagree, so whether a combined no-hitter counts is an unresolved reading and both readings are carried as branches (sstat_no_hitter_definition). Each market carries can_close_early true with early_close_condition 'This market will close and expire after the event occurs'; the 20-win and 50/50 markets closed 2026-09-28 and the other six on 2026-10-29 (close_time in the API object), all expecting expiration 2026-12-01. The listing shows three velocity events (105+, 106+, 107+) that the series assignment routes to the velocity archetype; the 105+ event returned no market object.

rules_evidence.quote: in any game during the 2026 Pro Baseball season (regular season and playoffs), then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Sampled KXMLBSTAT wording (velocity event KXMLBSTAT-26P107-AP) for the season-plus-playoffs window and any-player union; the events API wording for the single-game feats uses the same phrasing, but only this velocity event is in the sampled rules file.

variants_and_edge_cases: Single-game feats (perfect game, no hitter, 20+ strikeouts, 4+ HR, 2+ grand slams, 500+ ft HR) count regular season and playoffs, whereas the 20-win and 50/50 events count the regular season only (per the one-sentence API wording), so playoff exposure matters for six events and not for two.

All eight events are any-pitcher or any-hitter unions with a custom (not floor) strike construction; the probability is dominated by the league environment, and a feat that has already happened makes the market a pure settlement question.

'No hitter' versus 'Individual Pitcher No Hitter': the event title says individual, the rules text says 'any pitcher records a no hitter'; whether a combined no-hitter counts, and whether the game must go nine innings, is not stated, so both readings are carried and the market is not priced on an individual-only assumption (sstat_no_hitter_definition). Nesting: a perfect game is also a no-hitter, so P(perfect game) <= P(individual no-hitter) <= P(no-hitter under any reading).
'500+ foot home run (per Statcast measurement)' ties settlement to the tracked projected distance; rounding at exactly 500 and home runs without a recorded distance are not addressed.

KXMLBSTAT-26P105 is listed as an event but no market object was retrievable; the three velocity events (105+, 106+, 107+) are routed to pitch_velocity_extremes by event_routing and are not modelled here.
The 50/50 event requires 50+ home runs and 50+ steals by the same hitter in the same regular season; the 20-win event requires 20 wins by one pitcher; neither allows aggregation across players.

Market lifecycle (API object, retrieved 2026-11-09): can_close_early true with early_close_condition 'This market will close and expire after the event occurs'; the markets opened in February and March except the 106+ and 107+ velocity pair (2026-06-27), so the as-of state is mid-season in several snapshots and the feats-to-date ledger is the starting state.
contract.settlement_data_source: Not named in the rules text. The Kalshi events API lists settlement_sources ESPN, 'the Governing League' (mlb.com) and Fox Sports for each event (event metadata, not the rules); Statcast is named only for the 500-foot event.

mechanism.summary: The eight non-velocity KXMLBSTAT events are not one process. Six are single-game feats counted anywhere in baseball: a no-hitter (individual or combined: the rule says 'any pitcher', the title says individual, so both readings are carried), a perfect game, a 20-strikeout game, a four-home-run game, a two-grand-slam game and a 500-foot home run. For each, the chance the feat happens in the rest of the season is one minus the exponential of minus the sum, over remaining team-games (about 4,860 in a 162-game schedule across 2,430 games, plus the playoff games each club is expected to play), of a small per-game rate. That rate has its own chain: starter length and strikeout rate for 20 strikeouts, starter length, contact allowed, defence and scoring decisions for no-hitters and perfect games, per-PA home-run propensity, lineup slot and bases-loaded opportunities for multi-homer and multi-grand-slam games, and the tail of home-run distance for the 500-foot drive. Two events are individual accumulation races: any pitcher reaching 20 regular-season wins (wins to date plus remaining starts times a per-start win probability, a union over a handful of candidates) and any hitter reaching 50 home runs and 50 steals (remaining plate appearances times power and speed rates with an injury hazard). Because these are 'any player' unions, the probability is dominated by the league environment rather than any named star, a feat already recorded settles Yes immediately, and probability collapses toward zero when the season or the race path closes. The sampled rules text covers only the velocity events; the settlement of every event here rests on a one-sentence API wording whose finer definitions are not available, and this record states that explicitly.

stages.name: Event wording, window and scoring authority
stages.description: Each KXMLBSTAT event has its own one-sentence rule (fetched from the Kalshi events API on 2026-11-09, not part of the sampled rules file): the single-game feats and the 500-foot drive count the regular season and playoffs, while the 20-win and 50/50 events count the regular season only; 'any pitcher' or 'any hitter' makes each a union over the league. What is not defined is the feat itself: whether a combined no-hitter counts (the event title says individual), whether a perfect game or no-hitter needs nine innings, how a Statcast distance is rounded, and who rules on hit-versus-error. The official scorer's rulings and later scoring changes therefore sit inside the settlement.
stages.distribution: Categorical window and definition choice per event; the scoring decision is a rare binary on the last hit or error of a no-hit bid.

stages.name: League-wide rare-event hazard over remaining team-games
stages.description: For each single-game feat the probability of at least one occurrence from the as-of date is 1 - exp(-sum of per-game rates over remaining team-games). The rate depends on the season's league strikeout rate, home-run rate and starter length, fitted on 1990-2025 league-season counts (500-foot drives only in the Statcast era), and on regime changes such as the ball, pitch clock and rule set. Playoff games add exposure weighted by each club's chance of playing them. An event that has already occurred is certain; the market is then only a rules and settlement question.
stages.distribution: Poisson count of feats over remaining games; very small rates give near-linear growth in games, larger rates (an individual no-hitter) saturate by season end; the total is censored at the first occurrence.

stages.name: Pitching feats: no-hitter, perfect game and 20-strikeout game
stages.description: An individual-reading no-hitter needs one starter to survive roughly 27 outs without a hit (a combined no-hitter, which may also count, needs only that the staff allows no hit), so it is gated by the exit hazard (how often a starter is allowed to go the distance), by contact allowed and defence behind him, and by official scoring of close plays. A perfect game adds no walks, hit batters or errors. A 20-strikeout game needs a pitcher with an elite strikeout rate facing a high-whiff lineup and staying in for nine innings or more. All three live in the extreme right tail of starter innings, which has shortened in recent seasons.
stages.distribution: Compound of a very thin tail of nine-inning starts and a per-out survival probability; geometric-like decay in outs recorded for the individual reading (each additional out multiplies the rate by a factor below one, to be fitted); the combined reading has a thicker tail.

stages.name: Batting feats: 4-home-run game, 2-grand-slam game and 500-foot drive
stages.description: Four home runs in a game needs about four of the hitter's roughly four to five plate appearances to end in a home run, so the probability rises roughly with the fourth power of the per-PA rate and is concentrated in elite power hitters in hitter-friendly parks with wind and warm air. Two grand slams needs two bases-loaded plate appearances and two home runs in the same game, which is gated by opportunity rather than power alone. A 500-foot drive is the extreme tail of the home-run distance distribution and depends on exit velocity, launch angle, altitude and wind, and on how Statcast measures the projected distance.
stages.distribution: Binomial tail in per-PA home-run probability for multi-homer games; product of opportunity count and conversion for grand slams; generalised-Pareto tail for distance, with finite physical endpoint.

stages.name: Accumulation races: 20 wins and 50 home runs with 50 steals
stages.description: Twenty wins is a union over starters with wins to date W0, remaining starts n and a per-start win probability that combines the chance of five or more innings (starter exit hazard) with the team's lead at exit and bullpen holds; most candidates are eliminated by arithmetic once n times the achievable win rate falls short. Fifty home runs and fifty steals is a joint threshold for a rare power-speed hitter: remaining plate appearances come from games left, lineup slot and health, home runs and steals each follow shrunk rates and are coupled by a copula. Both races are regular-season only, so playoff games add nothing. Both races are any-player unions: P(any) = 1 - prod over candidate pitchers (or hitters) still arithmetically alive of (1 - p_candidate), so the number of live candidates matters as much as the best candidate's probability.
stages.distribution: Binomial-sum (Poisson-binomial) of remaining wins with an absorbing zero once the path closes; for 50/50, a negative-binomial pair coupled by a copula with a health-driven random exposure.

talent_strength.note: Strikeout and power talent of the few candidates that produce the feats.

opponent_matchup.note: The opposing lineup's whiff rate and contact quality shape 20-strikeout and no-hit chances; for the named-hitter races the opponent matters only through the aggregated rates.

role_personnel.note: Which pitchers start how often and which hitters get the plate appearances decide the two accumulation races.

availability_news.note: Injuries remove candidates from the 20-win and 50/50 races and from single-game exposure; the point-in-time vintage matters.

coaching_scheme.note: Managers' hook rules are the main modern constraint on complete games, no-hitters and 20-strikeout games.

environment.note: Park, altitude, wind and temperature scale home-run frequency and distance.

game_context_script.note: Bases-loaded states arise in high-scoring game scripts; no-hit bids also depend on game script via pitch counts.

pace_volume.note: Remaining team-games, playoff games and outs per start set exposure. The feats-to-date ledger gives the already-recorded events and the games played and remaining by regular season and playoffs.

efficiency_conversion.note: Per-opportunity conversion: grand slams per bases-loaded PA, hits per ball in play, steals per attempt opportunity.

distribution_variance.note: Poisson, binomial-sum and tail distributions of rare events and of two accumulation races. The any-player union across live candidates is in the race inputs.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Games remaining and September rest or skipped starts change late-season exposure; clinched-team rest is not separately attached.

officiating_rules.note: Hit-versus-error scoring and the rule and ball regime change what counts and how often.

settlement_contract.note: Window (regular season versus playoffs), any-player union, and feat definitions; the finer definitions are not stated and are listed as unresolved.

mlb.hr_distance_tail_exceedance.label: Home-run distance tail: per-home-run probability of a Statcast-measured projected distance of 500 feet or more, by hitter power, park altitude and conditions
mlb.hr_distance_tail_exceedance.mechanism: A 500-foot drive is an extreme-order statistic of the distance distribution of home runs: only the few hitters with extreme exit velocity and ideal launch angle, in thin air or with a tailwind, put real mass beyond 500 feet.
mlb.hr_distance_tail_exceedance.rationale: The contract says '(per Statcast measurement)', so what matters is the tracked projected distance of each home run, not eyeballed distance. The probability of one 500+ ft homer in a season is the sum over thousands of home runs of a tiny tail probability that is concentrated in a handful of hitters and a few high-altitude or wind-aided parks, so the tail must be fitted per hitter-park cell rather than from the league mean distance. The league-wide count of such drives is so small that it cannot be estimated by simple counting and is the most extrapolation-prone of the eight KXMLBSTAT feats.
mlb.hr_distance_tail_exceedance.measurement: From Statcast home-run rows (hit_distance_sc, launch_speed, launch_angle, park, game temperature) for 2015-2025 plus the current season: for every hitter with >= 150 batted balls in the last 3 seasons fit a generalised Pareto to the distance exceedances over u = 440 ft with a hitter-level scale driven by the 95th percentile of exit velocity (shrunk to league with k = 40 home runs) and a park-level shift from altitude and median game temperature. p_h,g = P(distance >= 500.0 | HR) x P(HR | PA) for hitter h in game g; expected 500+ ft drives for the rest of the season = sum over hitters and remaining team-games of PA_g x p_h,g, with remaining playoff games weighted by P(club plays them) from the bracket. Report the sensitivity to the GPD shape (xi between -0.3 and 0) because the observed exceedance count is tiny. Units: expected count and probability = 1 - exp(-sum). As-of: daily, using only home runs dated before the as-of date.

mlb.bases_loaded_pa_opportunity.label: Bases-loaded plate-appearance opportunity per hitter-game and grand-slam conversion rate
mlb.bases_loaded_pa_opportunity.mechanism: A grand slam needs a home run in a bases-loaded plate appearance, and two in one game need two such plate appearances for the same hitter, so opportunity (lineup slot, on-base quality of the hitters ahead, team run environment) multiplies the conversion rate.
mlb.bases_loaded_pa_opportunity.rationale: A season-long 'two grand slams in a game' event is gated twice: the hitter must come up with the bases full at least twice in one game, which is rare and concentrated in high-scoring games with strong on-base hitters ahead of a power bat, and must homer both times. Treating it as a generic multi-homer rate misses that the opportunity count, not power alone, is the scarce resource, and that pitchers with the bases loaded change approach (more walks, fewer middle-middle pitches).
mlb.bases_loaded_pa_opportunity.measurement: From Retrosheet event files 2015-2025: (a) q_slot = share of plate appearances by lineup slot with the bases loaded, as a function of team runs scored per game and the OBP of the three hitters ahead (logistic, shrunk to league with k = 2,000 PA); (b) per-hitter grand-slam conversion c_h = (grand slams_h + c_league x 100)/(bases-loaded PA_h + 100), i.e. shrunk toward the league conversion c_league with a prior weight of 100 bases-loaded PA; (c) distribution of bases-loaded PA per hitter-game as Poisson-binomial over the hitter's expected 4.2 PA with q varying by inning and game script. P(2+ GS in game) = sum over k >= 2 of P(K = k) x P(at least 2 conversions | k). Season probability = 1 - exp(-sum over remaining hitter-games of P(2+ GS)), cross-checked against the league-season count of 2+ grand-slam games since 1990. Units: probability per hitter-game. As-of: daily.

mlb.leaguewide_rare_game_event_hazard.label: League-wide single-game rare-event hazard over the remaining season and playoffs (individual no-hitter, perfect game, 4+ HR game, 20+ K game, 2+ grand slams in a game, 500+ ft Statcast home run)
mlb.leaguewide_rare_game_event_hazard.mechanism: Each 'any player' feat is a union over every remaining team-game of a tiny per-game probability, so its chance is one minus the survival of a low-rate point process whose rate depends on the league's strikeout and power environment and on how long starters pitch.
mlb.leaguewide_rare_game_event_hazard.rationale: Rates moved sharply across eras: higher strikeout rates raised no-hit and 20-strikeout chances per inning while shorter starts lowered the chance of one pitcher finishing 27 outs; multi-HR feats depend on the right tail of hitter power. The no-hitter definition is NOT settled by the contract: the rule says 'any pitcher records a no hitter' while the event title says 'Individual Pitcher No Hitter', and combined no-hitters are a material share of recent no-hitters (share not measured here), so this input carries the readings as explicit branches instead of assuming one. Using long-run historical averages without these adjustments misstates the hazard by large factors.
mlb.leaguewide_rare_game_event_hazard.measurement: For each event e and reading r, per team-game rate lambda_e,r(t) = exp(b0 + b1*league K% + b2*league HR per PA + b3*league mean starter outs per start) fitted by Poisson regression on league-season counts 1990-2025 (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED that every count is obtainable from Retrosheet and Baseball-Reference lists). Branches kept separately for the no-hitter: (A) one pitcher records all outs of a nine-inning game, (B) any no-hit game including combined and shortened games; the perfect game and 20-strikeout counts are single branches. Nested monotonicity is enforced: P(perfect game) <= P(no-hitter A) <= P(no-hitter B). The 500-ft drive, 4+ HR and 2+ grand-slam events are modelled bottom-up in mlb.hr_distance_tail_exceedance, mlb.hitter_hr_profile and mlb.bases_loaded_pa_opportunity; the league-count regression for those three is used only as a calibration cross-check against the bottom-up sum, never added to it. P(event in the rest of the season) = 1 - exp(-sum over remaining regular-season team-games and expected playoff team-games of lambda); playoff team-games count only for the six events that include the playoffs. Games already played are taken from the feats-to-date ledger (mlb.season_feat_ledger_state): an achieved feat settles Yes. Units: probability per branch. As-of: the market timestamp.

mlb.any_pitcher_season_wins_threshold.label: Any-pitcher 20-win season threshold: probability at least one pitcher reaches 20 regular-season wins
mlb.any_pitcher_season_wins_threshold.mechanism: A pitcher's wins accumulate one start at a time with a win credited only if he completes five innings with his team leading and the lead holds, so 20 wins needs a near-full rotation workload on a strong team and has become rare as starts shorten.
mlb.any_pitcher_season_wins_threshold.rationale: Wins depend on team offence and bullpen as much as on the pitcher, and on starts remaining; the union over pitchers is dominated by the two or three leaders by the deadline, and the event collapses once their remaining starts cannot close the gap, so a pace-based projection that ignores remaining rotation turns misprices it late in the season.
mlb.any_pitcher_season_wins_threshold.measurement: For each pitcher with W0 wins at the as-of date: remaining starts n_i from the rotation schedule (mlb.pitcher_rotation_slot_and_rest, five-man turns adjusted for off days and IL risk); per-start win probability p_i = P(starter records >= 15 outs) from the shared exit hazard (mlb.sp_hook_hazard_curve) x P(team leads when he exits and holds the lead) from his team's run-scoring and bullpen models, fitted on 2015-2025 starts with logistic calibration. W_i = W0 + Binomial(n_i, p_i) (Poisson-binomial when p varies by opponent); P(any >= 20) = 1 - product over pitchers of P(W_i < 20), assuming independence across teams and a shared-team correction for teammates. Units: probability; as-of the market timestamp, regular season only per the rules.

mlb.joint_season_hr_sb_distribution.label: Joint season HR-SB distribution for one hitter (power-speed profile, PA, availability)
mlb.joint_season_hr_sb_distribution.mechanism: A season with both H* home runs and S* steals (50 and 50 for KXMLBSTAT-265050, 50 and 40 for KXMLBSTATCOUNT) is a joint tail of two correlated counts requiring health and plate appearances; an any-hitter contract is the union of that joint tail over every hitter still on pace.
mlb.joint_season_hr_sb_distribution.rationale: The probability depends on each hitter's season-to-date pace, remaining PA and the rates of both events, and the two are correlated through playing time and hitter quality; independence misprices. For an any-hitter contract only a handful of hitters have both thresholds reachable, so the answer is dominated by the one or two power-speed candidates and by their health.
mlb.joint_season_hr_sb_distribution.measurement: Given current HR_0, SB_0, team games remaining G, per-game play probability from availability and PA per game by lineup slot, set rates r_HR and r_SB per PA = (ROS projection * 250 + season pace * n)/(250 + n) with n = season PA. Simulate 20,000 seasons: PA_rest from game draws with a health hazard; HR_rest ~ NegBin(mean r_HR*PA_rest, dispersion fitted across hitters 2015-2025) and SB_rest ~ NegBin(mean r_SB*PA_rest); couple the two with a Gaussian copula whose rho is the cross-hitter correlation of season HR and SB rate residuals given PA (2015-2025). Output p_h = P(HR_0 + HR_rest >= H* and SB_0 + SB_rest >= S*) for one hitter. For an any-hitter contract take the candidate set = hitters for whom both thresholds are still arithmetically reachable and compute P(any) = 1 - prod over candidates (1 - p_h), treating different clubs' hitters as independent. Units: probability. As-of: daily.

interactions.mechanism: Twenty strikeouts need both a very high strikeout rate per batter and enough batters faced, so the pitcher-level probability is the product of rate and depth; a pitcher with a high strikeout rate who is pulled early, or a deep pitcher with an ordinary rate, contributes little, and the two factors are estimated from different data.
interactions.how_to_test: Across starts since 1990, compare the observed frequency of 15+ strikeout games by cells of pitcher K% and batters faced against the product of the two marginal rates.

interactions.mechanism: Two grand slams in one game require two bases-loaded plate appearances and two home runs, so the probability is roughly the product of opportunity and conversion squared; a high-power hitter batting behind weak on-base hitters has little opportunity and a mid-power cleanup hitter in a high-scoring game has more.
interactions.how_to_test: Bucket historical hitter-games by number of bases-loaded plate appearances (0, 1, 2+) and compare the observed count of 2+ GS games with the product of opportunity and per-hitter conversion.

interactions.mechanism: The distance input carries altitude and temperature but not the wind component; a wind blowing out adds distance on top of altitude and exit velocity, and the tail beyond 500 feet is convex in the total shift, so a tailwind at a high-altitude park for a hitter with an extreme exit-velocity ceiling multiplies the chance more than the sum of the separate effects.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare the share of home runs beyond 450 feet by wind-out component within park-altitude and exit-velocity-tier cells, and test whether the odds ratio of the wind term grows with altitude.

interactions.mechanism: A candidate with W0 wins and n starts left can only reach 20 if W0 + n >= 20, and realistically if the needed win rate is attainable; late in the season the probability drops to zero in steps as candidates are eliminated, and an injury or skipped start removes starts in one jump.
interactions.how_to_test: Replay 2015-2025 seasons date by date and check that the model's P(any >= 20) is zero for dates when no candidate satisfies W0 + remaining starts >= 20.

interactions.mechanism: 50/50 requires both counts to reach 50 for the same hitter, and an injury lowers both through the shared plate-appearance exposure, so the joint probability is far below the product of the marginals when health is uncertain; the any-hitter union then adds the few candidates that the ledger still lists as alive, and a hitter on pace for only one half is not a partial candidate.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the joint distribution with and without a shared health hazard, take the union over the ledger's live candidates, and compare calibration with realised power-speed seasons by date.

interactions.mechanism: Whether a no-hit bid survives depends on borderline contacts: when contact allowed and defence are poor, many close plays are scored hits regardless of scorer, but a good defence with a lenient scorer converts borderline plays to errors that keep a no-hitter alive but break a perfect game.
interactions.how_to_test: Using official scoring of close plays in historical no-hit bids, compare the share ruled hits versus errors by park scorer and defence tier, and the difference in survival between no-hit and perfect-game bids.

nonlinearities.shape: concave saturating in remaining team-games: 1 - exp(-lambda x games)
nonlinearities.why: Early in the season a rare feat with a larger per-game rate (an individual no-hitter) is close to certain by year end while a smaller-rate event (perfect game, 4-HR game) stays modest; probability rises quickly with games remaining then saturates and drops to the realised outcome when the window closes.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold with an absorbing zero once W0 + remaining starts < 20
nonlinearities.why: The race is a union of binomial sums whose probability is a steep function of wins to date; one win or one skipped start changes a candidate from feasible to impossible, so the market moves in steps.

Physical limits on exit velocity and launch angle give the distance distribution a finite endpoint; a small change in the fitted shape changes the probability of 500 feet by large factors, so the response to hitter power is steeply nonlinear.

catalog_entry.target: Whether a named hitter records at least N home runs across a playoff series or at least one home run inside a fixed date window.
catalog_entry.mechanism: A named hitter's home runs over a playoff series or a date window are a sum over plate appearances of a small per-PA probability. Exposure is the number of games (random for a series, scheduled for a window), whether he starts and stays healthy, the plate appearances per game and the quality of the starters and relievers he faces; the per-PA probability is his regressed power times park, wind and pitcher adjustments. Counts of 2 or more are convex in exposure, while a one-or-more window event saturates for a healthy regular so that injury state dominates; neither contract has a start gate.

mechanism.summary: A named hitter's home-run count across a playoff series or inside a date window is a sum over his plate appearances of an event with a small per-PA probability, so the number of plate appearances is the first thing to model and the per-PA probability the second. For a date window, exposure is every team game between the dates, with off days, doubleheaders, injuries and role changes, and the probability of at least one home run saturates for healthy regulars so that the uncertainty becomes the health state. The per-PA probability is the hitter's power (barrels, fly-ball and pull-air rate, maximum exit velocity) regressed toward the league and adjusted for the pitcher's HR vulnerability by batter hand, park HR factor, wind and temperature. Counts of 2+ or more are convex in exposure, so series length and benching move them more than proportionally. Settlement follows official scoring of home runs, including inside-the-park and extra-inning home runs. Neither sampled text defines what happens if the player is injured or benched, so exposure simply disappears: a 2+ rung then fails arithmetically, while whether a missed series or window is void is not stated.

stages.name: Exposure frame: series boundaries versus date window
stages.description: Reading the wording fixes the exposure frame before anything else: one named playoff series of random length (the two clubs' per-game win probabilities decide whether it ends in four, five, six or seven games) or a calendar window of scheduled team games with off days and doubleheaders (KXMLBNEXTHR counts any MLB game between two dates). The rules do not define a start gate, so every plate appearance in the frame counts, and the number of games must be modelled as a distribution rather than a constant.
stages.distribution: Series length is a discrete distribution on 4-7 games with probability mass shifting to longer series for evenly matched clubs; window length is deterministic apart from postponements and doubleheaders.

stages.name: Participation: starts, roster and injury state
stages.description: The hitter must be on the round roster for a series, in the lineup in each game and still in the game for his plate appearances; platoon hitters start against one pitcher hand only. For a window the same chain runs over every scheduled game, with injury as an absorbing state until a return date. A hurt hitter's market is driven by the return timeline, and for a healthy regular the injury hazard per game, which compounds over a long window, is the main source of probability loss.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli start per game with a long-tailed absorbing injury state; mixture of a healthy branch and an injured branch with a return-date distribution.

stages.name: Plate appearances and pitcher quality faced
stages.description: Plate appearances per game depend on lineup slot and the game's run environment (about four to five for a regular lineup spot). Within a series the starters change by game after off days, so the hitter's PAs are split across the rotation and different bullpens: an ace on short rest, a bullpen game, or a left-handed starter for a platoon bat. Within a game, the plate appearances after the starter exits face relievers with a different HR rate and handedness. The per-game exposure is therefore a weighted sum over pitcher types, not a constant.
stages.distribution: Per-game PA count approximately Poisson-binomial around 4-5; pitcher mix is a categorical assignment per game with probabilities from the rotation schedule.

stages.name: Per-PA home-run probability: power, park and conditions
stages.description: The per-PA probability of a home run is the hitter's regressed power rate (barrels, fly-ball and pull-air rate, maximum exit velocity) multiplied by the park HR factor for his handedness and by wind and temperature at first pitch, and adjusted for the opposing pitcher type from stage 3. Rates are small (a few percent per PA for elite power hitters), so the observed record over a short window or series is dominated by chance and carries little information beyond the profile.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli per PA with probability a few percent; the sum over PAs is Poisson-binomial with dispersion from shared game conditions (wind, ball, pitcher day).

stages.name: Aggregation to the contract threshold and ladder
stages.description: P(at least k home runs) for the series is a compound sum over the random number of games of per-game Poisson-binomial counts; for the window market the probability of at least one is one minus the product over scheduled games of (1 - participation x per-game HR probability) with an injury absorbing state. Higher rungs (2+, 3+) are convex in total exposure so the ladder spreads out as series length grows; the one-or-more window event saturates and is close to one for a healthy power hitter over a long window.
stages.distribution: Compound sum over a random game count for series counts; survival product with absorbing injury for window one-or-more; right-censored at the window end.

interactions.mechanism: A 2+ rung needs two events, so its probability rises faster than linearly in total plate appearances: a seven-game series instead of a four-game series roughly doubles the chance of one home run but more than triples the chance of two, and the effect is larger for hitters with higher per-PA power.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare realised series home-run rungs against a linear-in-games model, split by series length and hitter power tier, over 2012-2025 playoff series.

interactions.mechanism: In a date window a healthy power hitter's probability of at least one home run saturates within a few weeks, so almost all remaining uncertainty is the injury state: a hitter on the injured list with an uncertain return has a probability governed by return timing rather than by power.
interactions.how_to_test: Split historical windows by injured-list status at the as-of date and compare realised hit rates with a power-only model.

interactions.mechanism: A platoon hitter starts against one pitcher hand and his exposure is concentrated in the games where the opposing starter is of the favourable hand; the rotation order after off days therefore changes both his start probability and the vulnerability of the pitcher he faces, and the two effects are correlated.
interactions.how_to_test: For platoon hitters in past series, regress per-game start and HR on opposing starter hand and starter HR/FB, and test the interaction.

interactions.mechanism: Park and weather scale the per-PA rate multiplicatively for fly-ball pull hitters; wind blowing out in a hitter-friendly park raises the rate most for hitters with high pull-air rate, while the HR/FB regression pulls extreme observed rates back toward true talent.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit per-PA HR logit with interaction between pull-air rate and park-wind factor on 2015-2025 Statcast, comparing with an additive model.

interactions.mechanism: A series market for an injured hitter switches regime on roster submission: before it, P(on roster) is a mixture over return timelines; after it, the probability is zero or one and the injury-replacement rule decides whether he can return in later rounds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare the realised round-roster inclusion of injured-list hitters before and after submission across 2012-2025 postseasons.

nonlinearities.shape: convex in plate appearances for 2+ rungs, near-linear for 1+
nonlinearities.why: Two home runs are needed, so the probability grows roughly with the square of exposure at low rates; series length and benching move it more than proportionally.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating 1 - prod(1 - p_g): concave in games for a healthy hitter
nonlinearities.why: A one-or-more window event saturates as games accumulate, so extra games add little for a regular and almost nothing after the first few weeks; the market is then about injury, not power.

nonlinearities.shape: convex in barrel and pull-air rate
nonlinearities.why: Home-run probability per PA rises faster than linearly in barrel rate and exit-velocity ceiling, so the gap between an elite power hitter and a regular is large in a short exposure.

catalog_entry.label: MLB pitcher consecutive scoreless innings streak
catalog_entry.target: Whether a named pitcher reaches N consecutive scoreless innings from a streak start through the end of the regular season.
catalog_entry.mechanism: A pitcher's chance of reaching N consecutive scoreless innings from a stated start date is a survival product over the outs still needed: 3N outs in a row with no run charged. It depends on the as-of total already banked, the starts and outs per start remaining before the regular season ends, the per-inning scoreless probability against each opponent (talent, lineup, park, defence, sequencing), exit-state and inherited-runner charging, and a luck regression because pitchers selected on a streak have benefited from strand, BABIP and home-run luck. The first run ends the streak and settles all unreached rungs No.

inputs.why: Core survival engine: per-out probability of no run charged and P(reach N innings) from the carried streak over remaining starts.
As-of streak state: outs already credited since the stated start date, whether the streak is alive, runs counted by the contract's definition and starts left.
Number and timing of remaining starts before the regular season ends caps the outs available.
Outs per start from the shared exit hazard, including whether a manager pulls a streaking starter early.
Runners left on base who score after the starter exits are charged to him and can end the streak.
Run expectancy conversion of baserunners by base-out state turns hits and walks into runs.
Unearned-run share decides how often an error produces a run that may or may not end the streak, depending on how the contract counts runs.
True-talent quality of the pitcher (SIERA, xFIP, Stuff+) sets the run-prevention probability per inning.
Strand-rate luck during the streak is mean-reverting and must be regressed out of the per-inning scoreless probability.
BABIP luck during the streak likewise reverts and biases the observed scoreless rate.
Out-rate profile of the lineups in the remaining starts sets per-inning survival by opponent.
Defence behind the pitcher and contact allowed convert balls in play into baserunners.
Clinched or eliminated status changes late-season rest, skipped starts and starter innings.
IL status and late scratches pause or end exposure; a pitcher who misses starts cannot extend the streak.
Home runs are the single most damaging way to break a scoreless inning; HR/FB regression tempers lucky low-HR streaks.
Streak definition: partial innings at one third, nested rungs, regular season end and the Apr 30 start stated in the wording.

interactions.hypothesis: A streak can only reach N if enough starts and outs remain: late in the season a rung becomes impossible once remaining starts times outs per start plus the carried total falls below N, however dominant the pitcher is, and the probability falls in steps as each start is used.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute the maximum attainable streak from remaining starts and outs per start by date and check that historical rungs beyond it never settled Yes.

interactions.hypothesis: Runners a streaking pitcher leaves on base and who later score are charged to him and, if the contract counts all charged runs, break the streak; managers protecting a streak pull him with bases empty, so bullpen strand rate and exit-state policy change survival late in starts.
interactions.how_to_test: In historical long streaks compare the share of streak-ending runs scored by inherited runners with the share expected from typical exit states.

interactions.hypothesis: During a long streak the observed run prevention exceeds what pitcher quality supports, so the weight placed on the streak's own rates versus true talent should switch toward talent as the gap grows; ignoring this overstates persistence for pitchers selected on luck.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest continuation probabilities for all pitchers at 30+ innings of scoreless streak since 1990 against models that use observed versus talent-regressed rates.

interactions.hypothesis: If the contract counts only earned runs, errors and passed balls extend the streak and per-inning survival is higher; if it counts all runs, the unearned share adds hazard; because the text is silent the survival product is a two-branch mixture weighted by the probability of each reading.
interactions.how_to_test: On historical streaks, compare lengths under an all-runs versus an earned-runs definition and count how often an unearned run ended a streak.

contract.settlement_definition: KXMLBSISTREAK settles YES if the named pitcher (sample: Cristopher Sanchez, 70+ innings) records at least the strike number of consecutive scoreless innings 'from the start of his streak (Apr 30, 2026) until either the streak ends or the 2026 Pro Baseball regular season concludes, whichever comes first'. Scoreless innings are cumulative and count partial innings, each scoreless out counting one third of an inning. If the streak is broken, 'all markets that have not been achieved yet will resolve to No', so the rungs are nested and settle as soon as reached. The text does not say whether an unearned run, or a run charged to the pitcher through an inherited runner after he exits, breaks the streak, whether relief appearances count towards the streak, or how a pitcher who goes on the injured list settles; the rule also stops at the end of the regular season, so postseason innings are excluded.

rules_evidence.quote: each scoreless out counts as 1/3 of an inning toward the total streak
rules_evidence.establishes: The streak is measured in outs: reaching N innings needs 3N consecutive outs recorded with no run charged.

rules_evidence.quote: If Cristopher Sanchez's consecutive scoreless innings streak is broken, then all markets that have not been achieved yet will resolve to No.
rules_evidence.establishes: A single run ends the streak and settles every unreached rung No, so the rungs are nested absorbing barriers.

rules_evidence.quote: from the start of his streak (Apr 30, 2026)
rules_evidence.establishes: The count runs from a stated start date; the as-of cumulative total at the market's open is part of the contract state.

rules_evidence.quote: until either the streak ends or the 2026 Pro Baseball regular season concludes, whichever comes first
rules_evidence.establishes: Exposure is capped by the remaining regular-season starts; postseason innings do not count.

variants_and_edge_cases: Rungs are nested thresholds on one streak (the sample is the 70+ rung, floor_strike 70, strike_type greater_or_equal); a rung settles YES the moment it is reached and every higher rung settles No when the streak breaks, so the ladder is monotone and correlated with the streak state.

The text does not say whether the streak counts only starts or also relief outs, whether the streak breaks on an unearned run, or on a run charged to the pitcher for an inherited runner who scores after he leaves; these definitions change per-inning survival materially.

The window ends when the regular season concludes: the streak cannot be extended in the postseason, so remaining regular-season starts (a starter makes roughly 30 starts in a full season, so only a few remain late in the year) bound the maximum attainable length.

A pitcher placed on the injured list is not addressed by the text; inferred, not stated: missing starts reduces the outs available rather than ending the streak, and a return before the season ends could resume it. This reading is declared unresolved (sis_postseason_and_injury).
Only one rung (70+) and one pitcher (Sanchez, streak start Apr 30, 2026) were sampled; other pitchers and start dates may use the same wording but the count to date is as-of state.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official MLB box scores and play-by-play (runs charged, outs recorded); the sampled text names only 'the Governing League' and does not define run charging.

mechanism.summary: A scoreless-innings streak target of N innings from a stated start is a survival problem over outs. Reaching N needs 3N consecutive outs with no run scoring, so the probability is the product, across the outs still required, of per-out survival; because runs come in clusters (baserunners then hits and home runs) the per-inning scoreless probability is the natural unit, assumed here to be roughly 0.75 to 0.85 for the best starters and lower on average (both figures are modelling assumptions to be fitted, not sourced), so even a 100-percent-healthy ace has a probability that decays geometrically with the remaining gap. The streak-start state matters: the as-of cumulative total since the start date, whether the streak is alive, and how the contract counts runs (earned versus unearned, inherited runners) set the gap that remains. Three exposure constraints bound the attainable length: the number of starts left before the regular season ends (rotation slot, rest, skipped starts, an injury), the innings per start (exit hazard, the manager's willingness to pull a streaking starter or pitch him deep), and run prevention in each start (opponent lineup, park, defence and sequencing luck). Luck is the central modelling hazard: long streaks are selected on low BABIP, high strand rate and few home runs, all of which regress, so the survival model must regress the pitcher's observed rates harder when he is already on a streak. The streak ends at the first run, and rungs above the current length settle No at that moment while the rung just reached settles Yes at once.

stages.name: Streak definition and as-of state
stages.description: Before modelling, the contract fixes the stated streak start (Apr 30, 2026), the unit (outs at one third of an inning), the end (a run or the end of the regular season) and the nested rungs. The as-of state is the cumulative outs credited since the start date, whether the streak is currently alive and which run definition (all runs versus earned runs) is applied; because the text is silent on unearned and inherited runs, the state must be kept under both readings. A market opened mid-streak is a conditional problem from the carried total.
stages.distribution: Deterministic state (outs credited so far) plus a binary alive flag; ambiguity in the run definition creates a two-branch mixture of the survival product.

stages.name: Remaining starts and outs per start
stages.description: The number of starts left before the regular season ends and the outs recorded per start bound the maximum streak: remaining starts come from the rotation slot, days of rest, off-day skipping and the chance of a skipped or shortened start, while outs per start come from the exit hazard and from the manager's behaviour toward a streaking pitcher (protecting the streak by pulling him with the bases empty, or letting him go deep). Late in the season clinched or eliminated status can reduce innings, and an injury pauses the exposure. The maximum attainable streak is remaining starts times outs per start plus the carried total.
stages.distribution: Remaining starts is a discrete count with injury and skip risk (a small number of starts left late in the year); outs per start approximately 15-21 for a starter with a right-skewed tail.

stages.name: Per-inning scoreless probability against each opponent
stages.description: For each upcoming start the per-inning scoreless probability is built from a base-out state chain: the pitcher's strikeout, walk and home-run rates regressed to talent, the opposing lineup's out-rate, park run environment, defence behind him, and the conversion of runners to runs. The chain gives the probability of getting three outs before a run for each inning and, compounded over innings and starts, the survival curve. Home runs are the most damaging single event because they score regardless of baserunners.
stages.distribution: Per-inning scoreless probability assumed around 0.7-0.85 for good starters (assumption, to be fitted); geometric-like decay in innings, with variance from sequencing clusters rather than independent outs.

stages.name: Luck regression for a pitcher selected on a streak
stages.description: A pitcher on a long scoreless streak has by construction benefited from a high strand rate, low BABIP and a low HR/FB rate, all of which regress toward the league over the next starts, so the observed per-inning rate during the streak overstates the future rate. The survival model must replace the streak's observed rates with talent-based rates, with heavier shrinkage the more the pitcher's run suppression exceeds what his strikeout, walk and batted-ball quality imply.
stages.distribution: Selection bias in the observed rates (a winner's curse); the correction is a shrinkage factor with uncertainty from small samples.

stages.name: Exit-state, inherited runners and nested settlement
stages.description: When the starter leaves with runners on base, the relievers' strand rate decides whether those runners score and whether the runs are charged to the starter; managers protecting a streak may pull him with the bases empty. An error that produces a run may be unearned, and whether it breaks the streak depends on the contract's wording, which is silent. The nested rungs mean P(reach N) is a decreasing function of N that settles immediately when the streak breaks.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli per departing runner with probability set by reliever strand rate; unearned share small but not negligible (a few percent of runs).

mlb.scoreless_streak_ledger_state.label: Scoreless-streak ledger: cumulative outs since the stated streak start, alive flag, run definition applied and starts remaining as of the market timestamp
mlb.scoreless_streak_ledger_state.mechanism: The probability of reaching N innings depends on how many consecutive scoreless outs the pitcher has already banked, which is a state variable reconstructed from play-by-play from the stated start date, not a forecast.
mlb.scoreless_streak_ledger_state.rationale: The contract counts from a fixed start date (Apr 30, 2026) with partial innings at one third, so the as-of total is not simply 'current streak' in a data feed: it depends on whether relief outs are included, how runs are charged (earned versus all runs, inherited runners) and whether the streak is still alive. The same pitcher can have different totals under the two run readings, which is exactly the ambiguity the contract leaves open, so both ledgers must be kept.
mlb.scoreless_streak_ledger_state.measurement: From play-by-play since the stated start date build, for each pitcher-appearance, the sequence of outs recorded and runs charged (a) counting all runs charged to the pitcher including inherited runners who score, and (b) counting earned runs only; streak total_outs = outs recorded since the start date up to but excluding the first run under each reading, alive = no run charged under that reading, remaining_outs_needed = max(0, 3N - total_outs). Also store the number of regular-season team games remaining and the pitcher's projected starts left from mlb.pitcher_rotation_slot_and_rest. Flag any appearance in which official scoring was later changed (error to hit, earned-run reassignment): re-pull each appearance after a lag chosen by an observed revision study, because no source stating an official scoring-correction window was found (the 48 hours assumed earlier was unsourced). Run charging and inherited-runner attribution must be taken from a source that exposes them (MLB Stats API play-by-play or Retrosheet event files; field availability is SOURCE_UNVERIFIED here). Units: outs and a binary alive flag per reading. As-of: after every appearance and after each re-pull.

mlb.scoreless_streak_ledger_state.why: Isolates the state variable that the survival engine takes as input and the ambiguity in how the contract counts runs; the generic survival input does not store the ledger under both readings.

mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.label: Scoreless-streak survival: per-out probability a pitcher records an out with no run charged, and P(reach N innings) from the current streak
mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.mechanism: A scoreless streak extends by one third of an inning per out recorded without a run charged to the pitcher and ends at the first charged run, so reaching N is a survival product over the outs still needed.
mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.rationale: KXMLBSISTREAK settles on consecutive scoreless innings counted in thirds; elite starters post per-inning scoreless rates near 0.80, so a ten-inning gap has probability around 0.1 and is extremely sensitive to the per-inning rate, opponents, parks and whether runners he leaves on base later score. The contract does not say whether unearned runs break the streak, so both definitions must be computed.
mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.measurement: Define the streak in outs. For each future outing j compute, by dynamic programming over the 24 base-out states within each half-inning, the probability S_j(k) of recording k consecutive outs with no run charged to the pitcher (counting all runs, and separately earned runs only). Transition probabilities from the pitcher's projected K%, BB%, HR/PA and BABIP vs the opponent lineup and park, each shrunk to league with k = 300 batters faced. Outs per outing from mlb.sp_hook_hazard_curve. P(reach N) = P(streak of N innings completed) summed over the outings remaining before season end by recursion on the carried streak. Add P(inherited runner scores) from bullpen strand rate. Units: probability. As-of: after each outing.

mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.why: Core survival engine over outs from the carried streak, with strand and home-run luck regressed.

mlb.sp_hook_hazard_curve.reason: Outs per start for a streaking pitcher come from the shared exit hazard, with an added manager effect when the streak is long; it sets how fast outs accumulate before the season ends.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: True-talent quality sets the per-inning scoreless probability that the survival chain compounds; its projection components should be used rather than the streak's observed rates.

mlb.lob_strand_luck.reason: Strand-rate luck is the main reason a pitcher selected on a streak overstates his future scoreless rate; it is the regression term, not a driver of the baseline.

mlb.babip_luck.reason: BABIP luck during the streak reverts and biases the observed scoreless rate; second order next to strand and home-run luck so context.

mlb.opposing_lineup_out_rate_profile.reason: Out-rate profile of the lineups in the remaining starts sets per-inning survival by opponent; should use confirmed lineups when available.

mlb.contact_defense.reason: Defence behind the pitcher converts balls in play to outs or baserunners; useful context but captured partly by the BABIP regression.

mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.reason: Clinched or eliminated status changes late-season rest and innings; relevant only in the last weeks of the regular season.

mlb.hrfb_regression.reason: Home runs are the most damaging way to end a scoreless inning, so the HR/FB regression tempers lucky streaks; context because the survival input already carries a home-run rate.

mlb.er_ur_scoring_split.reason: Unearned-run share decides how often an error-driven run occurs and whether it ends the streak under an all-runs reading; the contract text is silent so this input matters for the branch weights.

mlb.injuries_pit.reason: IL status and late scratches pause or end a pitcher's exposure to extend the streak; a point-in-time vintage avoids leaking later returns.

m.rules_text.reason: One-third-inning credit, nested rungs, the stated start date and the regular-season end all come from the wording; a settlement input, not a market price.

mlb.pitcher_rotation_slot_and_rest.reason: Remaining starts before the regular season ends cap the outs available; the input gives P(start on date) with off-day skip and announced-probable status.

mlb.inherited_runner_charge_risk.reason: Inherited runners who score after the starter exits are charged to him; the input gives expected extra earned runs after exit.

mlb.baserunner_to_run_conversion.reason: RE24-allowed by base-out state converts baserunners into runs, the core transition of the per-inning chain.

mlb.scoreless_streak_survival.reason: The survival engine over outs is the right object; its shrinkage constants and selection-on-luck treatment are open (sis_streak_persistence).

mlb.sp_workload.reason: Expected outs per start; superseded for this archetype by the shared exit-hazard curve, so context.

mlb.leash.reason: Hook tendency is a component of the shared exit hazard; here it matters through a manager's willingness to protect a streaking pitcher.

mlb.team_wrc_vs_hand.reason: Opposing lineup offence by handedness supports the out-rate profile of each upcoming opponent.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: Confirmed lineups sharpen the opponent profile for the next start only.

mlb.pitcher_hr_vulnerability.reason: HR/FB and barrels allowed set the home-run component of the per-inning run probability.

mlb.umpire.reason: Zone effects shift walk and strikeout rates slightly; no first-order effect on a multi-start streak.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Reliever quality decides whether runners left by the starter score and are charged to him.

mlb.park.reason: Park run and home-run environment of each upcoming start enters the per-inning scoreless probability.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Game-time weather scales run and home-run environment for each start.

m.ladder_structure.reason: Cross-rung price consistency is a market benchmark, not an input to the streak survival.

interactions.mechanism: A streak can only reach N if enough starts and outs remain: late in the season a rung becomes impossible once remaining starts times outs per start plus the carried total falls below N, however dominant the pitcher is, and the probability falls in steps as each start is used.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute the maximum attainable streak from remaining starts and outs per start by date and check that historical rungs beyond it never settled Yes.

interactions.mechanism: Runners a streaking pitcher leaves on base and who later score are charged to him and, if the contract counts all charged runs, break the streak; managers protecting a streak pull him with bases empty, so bullpen strand rate and exit-state policy change survival late in starts.
interactions.how_to_test: In historical long streaks compare the share of streak-ending runs scored by inherited runners with the share expected from typical exit states.

interactions.mechanism: During a long streak the observed run prevention exceeds what pitcher quality supports, so the weight placed on the streak's own rates versus true talent should switch toward talent as the gap grows; ignoring this overstates persistence for pitchers selected on luck.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest continuation probabilities for all pitchers at 30+ innings of scoreless streak since 1990 against models that use observed versus talent-regressed rates.

interactions.mechanism: If the contract counts only earned runs, errors and passed balls extend the streak and per-inning survival is higher; if it counts all runs, the unearned share adds hazard; because the text is silent the survival product is a two-branch mixture weighted by the probability of each reading.
interactions.how_to_test: On historical streaks, compare lengths under an all-runs versus an earned-runs definition and count how often an unearned run ended a streak.

interactions.mechanism: Per-inning scoreless probability is multiplicative in pitcher quality, lineup out rate and defence: a strong pitcher facing a weak lineup with a good defence stacks the three, while a single weak link (a poor defence, a power-heavy lineup) lowers survival across all innings of the start.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit per-inning scoreless logit with pitcher, opponent and defence terms on 2015-2025 starts and test the interaction between pitcher quality and lineup out rate.

nonlinearities.why: Each inning survives with probability q, so P(reach N) is about q to the power of the innings needed; a change in q from 0.78 to 0.82 multiplies the chance of a ten-inning gap by (0.82/0.78)^10, about 1.65, and the relative effect grows with the length of the gap.
The number of remaining starts is an integer that falls by one every five or six days, and a skipped start or an injury removes a full start's worth of outs in one jump.

nonlinearities.shape: convex regression toward the league mean in the strand rate
nonlinearities.why: Extreme strand rates during a streak regress strongly, so the adjustment is larger for pitchers further above the league average than for those near it.
